name: pwd
summary: Print the directory you are currently in.

examples.title: Show the current directory
examples.explain: Prints an absolute path that starts with /. Relative paths you type are resolved from here.

examples.title: Show the real path with symlinks resolved
examples.explain: If you entered the directory through a symbolic link, plain pwd shows the link path; -P shows the physical directory.

name: cd

install.note: Shell builtin; it must be, because a separate program cannot change your shell's directory.

compat: cd - and ~ work in bash, dash and BusyBox ash.

examples.title: Enter a directory
examples.explain: Relative paths start from the current directory; absolute paths start with /. 'No such file or directory' usually means a typo or wrong starting directory; check with pwd and ls.

examples.title: Enter a directory whose name contains spaces
examples.explain: Without quotes the shell would split this into two arguments, My and Projects. Quotes (or a backslash before the space) keep it as one name.

examples.title: Go up one level, home, or back
examples.explain: .. is the parent directory. cd with no argument (or cd ~) goes to your home directory; cd - jumps back to the previous directory and prints it.

name: ls
summary: List directory contents, with sizes, permissions, owners and dates.

install.note: Alpine and most embedded systems use the BusyBox ls by default.

compat: BusyBox ls supports the common short options (-l -a -h -t -r -d) but not every GNU long option. Do not parse ls output in scripts; use find or a shell glob instead.

examples.title: Long listing including hidden files
examples.explain: Names starting with . are hidden by default; -a shows them, including . (this dir) and .. (parent).
examples.output: Columns: type and permissions (e.g. -rw-r--r--, first character d = directory, l = symlink), link count, owner, group, size in bytes, modification time, name.
options: Long format: one file per line with details
Include entries whose names start with .

examples.title: Human-readable sizes
examples.explain: Sizes show as 4.0K, 12M, 1.1G instead of raw bytes. Note: a directory's size is the size of its entry list, not of its contents; use du for that.
options: Print sizes with K, M, G suffixes (with -l)

examples.title: Newest files last
examples.explain: -t sorts by modification time newest first, -r reverses it so the most recently changed files end up at the bottom, next to your prompt.

examples.title: Show a directory itself, not its contents
examples.explain: Useful for checking a directory's permissions and owner.
options: List directories themselves, not their contents

name: mkdir
summary: Create directories, including missing parent directories.
compat: -p and -m are POSIX and work in BusyBox.

examples.title: Create a directory
examples.explain: Fails with 'File exists' if the name is taken, and with 'No such file or directory' if a parent directory is missing.

examples.title: Create a whole path at once
examples.explain: -p creates every missing parent and does not complain if the directory already exists, which makes it safe to repeat in scripts and Makefiles.
options: Create parent directories as needed; no error if it exists

examples.title: Create a private directory
examples.explain: Only you (the owner) can read, enter or write it. The mode is applied directly instead of being reduced by your umask.
options: Set permission bits on creation (rwx for owner only)

name: touch
summary: Create an empty file, or update a file's timestamps.
compat: The -d date parsing shown below is GNU-specific; BusyBox accepts a narrower set of date formats.

examples.title: Create an empty file (or refresh its timestamp)
examples.explain: If the file exists its contents are untouched and only its modification time changes. make uses timestamps, so touching a source file forces it to rebuild.

examples.title: Set a specific modification time
examples.explain: Handy for testing scripts that look for old or new files.
options: Use the given date string instead of now (GNU)

name: cp
compat: -i, -r and -p work in BusyBox. -a is supported by GNU and BusyBox cp but is not POSIX.

examples.title: Copy a file, asking before overwriting
examples.explain: If <destination> is an existing directory the file is copied into it. With -i you get a prompt instead of a silent overwrite.
examples.warning: Without -i, cp replaces an existing destination file with no confirmation and no undo.

examples.title: Make a quick backup copy before editing
examples.explain: Simple and effective before changing a config file. Restore it later by copying it back.

examples.title: Copy a directory tree, keeping modes and times
examples.explain: -a (archive) copies recursively and preserves permissions, timestamps and symbolic links. If <destination-dir> exists, the source is copied inside it as a subdirectory.
examples.warning: Files with the same name in the destination are overwritten. Check the destination with ls first.
options: Archive: recursive, preserve attributes, keep symlinks as links

name: mv
summary: Move or rename files and directories.
compat: -i is POSIX; -n (never overwrite) is supported by GNU and BusyBox.

examples.title: Rename a file, asking before overwriting
examples.explain: Renaming within the same file system is instant and keeps the file's contents and permissions.
examples.warning: Without -i, an existing <new-name> is replaced silently.

examples.title: Move files into a directory
examples.explain: The trailing / makes the intent clear: if <dir> does not exist you get an error instead of a file renamed to <dir>.

name: rm
summary: Delete files and directories. There is no recycle bin.
compat: Deleted files are not moved to a trash folder; recovery is generally not possible. GNU rm refuses to operate on / by default, but that does not protect anything else.

examples.title: Look before you delete
examples.explain: Inspect-first workflow: confirm the exact names, and that a wildcard matches only what you expect, before running rm. Tip: echo rm *.o prints what the wildcard expands to without deleting anything.

examples.title: Delete a file, with confirmation
examples.explain: Asks 'remove regular file ...?' for each file; answer y to delete.
examples.warning: Deletion is permanent. Check the name with ls first, especially when using wildcards such as *.

examples.title: Delete a file whose name starts with a dash
examples.explain: -- ends option parsing: everything after it is treated as a file name, so a file named -rf is deleted instead of being read as options. Many commands support --.
examples.warning: Deletion is permanent. Confirm the name with ls -la first.
options: End of options; following arguments are names even if they start with -

examples.title: Remove an empty directory
examples.explain: rmdir only works on empty directories, so it cannot accidentally delete contents. 'Directory not empty' means files remain inside.

examples.title: Delete a directory and everything inside it
examples.explain: -r descends into the directory; -i asks about each file. Preview first with find <dir> | head -n 50. Use a path relative to where you are, and run pwd to be sure where that is.
examples.warning: Recursive deletion removes the whole tree permanently. Never point it at /, ~, a system directory, or a variable that might be empty (rm -r "$DIR/" with an empty DIR becomes rm -r /).
options: Recursive: remove directories and their contents

name: ln
summary: Create links, most commonly symbolic links (shortcuts) to files or directories.
compat: Argument order is target first, then link name, like cp. A relative target is resolved relative to the link's directory, not your current directory.

examples.title: Create a symbolic link
examples.explain: <link-name> becomes a pointer to <target>. Deleting the link does not touch the target; deleting the target leaves a broken (dangling) link.
options: Make a symbolic link instead of a hard link

examples.title: See where a link points
examples.explain: Prints the final absolute path after following every link. ls -l also shows 'name -> target'.
options: Follow every link and print the canonical path

name: stat
summary: Show detailed metadata of a file: size, permissions in octal, owner, inode and timestamps.
compat: The -c format option works in GNU and BusyBox stat. macOS/BSD stat uses different options.

examples.title: Show all metadata
examples.explain: Access shows permissions as both octal (0644) and symbolic (-rw-r--r--). Modify is when the contents changed, Change is when metadata (permissions, owner) changed.

examples.title: Print just octal permissions, owner and name
examples.explain: Custom format: %a octal mode, %U owner name, %n file name, %s size in bytes.

name: file
summary: Identify what kind of data a file contains: text, ELF binary (and for which CPU), image, archive...

install.note: Often absent from minimal containers and embedded images.

compat: Output wording differs between versions; read it, do not parse it exactly.

examples.title: Check what a file really is
examples.explain: Looks at the contents, not the extension. A compiled program shows something like 'ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64'.

examples.title: Check that a cross-compiled binary targets the board
examples.explain: For an embedded target you want to see the board's architecture, e.g. 'ARM, EABI5' or 'ARM aarch64'. If it says x86-64 you built with the host compiler, and the board will reply 'Exec format error' or 'not found'.
examples.output: Also check 'dynamically linked, interpreter /lib/ld-linux...': if that loader is missing on the target, running the program fails with 'not found' even though the file exists.

examples.title: Print only the MIME type
examples.explain: Prints e.g. text/plain or application/x-executable; easier to use in scripts.
options: Print the MIME type instead of a description

name: realpath
summary: Print the absolute, canonical path of a file.
compat: BusyBox realpath supports no options; --relative-to is GNU only.

examples.title: Get the full path of a file
examples.explain: Resolves ., .. and symbolic links. Useful when another tool needs an absolute path.

examples.title: Compute a relative path between two locations
examples.explain: Prints <path> as seen from <base-dir>, for example ../include/foo.h.
options: Print the result relative to this directory (GNU)
